country.comment: The study examines water and sanitation provision in the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Region (BAMR) in Argentina.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Abstract, and Section 1; PDF p. 3, Section 3

effect_estimate.comment: No econometric or inferential statistical model is estimated; the authors synthesize institutional, contractual, tariff, and coverage figures across BAMR operators and before/after AASA's post-1997 contractual and pro-poor adaptations.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported (descriptive institutional figures only). Across the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Region (circa 2005), historically rooted institutional fragmentation across 9 official suppliers and 2 regulators (ETOSS and ORAB) yielded stark disparities in coverage and access conditions: AASA served 7.8 million of ~10 million inhabitants with water and 5.8 million with sanitation, compared with 30% served (540,000 of 1.8 million) in AGBA, 850,000 of 2.3 million in ABSA, 60% water (65,000 of 120,000) and 48,000 sanitation in Sudamericana de Aguas (Pilar), and 75% water / 40% sanitation in Marcos Paz (43,400 inhabitants). Within AASA's concession, initial 1993 rules ('user pays' infrastructure charges, limiting service obligation to 'legally urbanised zones' which excluded ~500,000 shanty-town residents, centralized single-technology rules, and single-provider exclusivity) impeded expansion to low-income peripheral areas, whereas subsequent regulatory and contractual adaptations reduced splintering: the 1997 SUMA/CIS cross-subsidy renegotiation lowered average bi-monthly bills for newly connected water users from 60.69 pesos to 15.92 pesos (while increasing already-connected users' bills from 37.26 to 44.52 pesos), and participatory pro-poor schemes (MPG and Agua + Trabajo, alongside 4 to 6.5 peso bi-monthly tariff deductions) connected 520,000 inhabitants of deprived neighbourhoods between 2000 and 2005 (120,000 via MPG and 400,000 via Agua + Trabajo).
